title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook: Process, Runbooks, Postmortems, Rotations, Game Days, Status & Comms Templates
author: Aisha Ramos
content:
Overview

This playbook documents Redwood Inference’s formal on-call and incident response process, runbooks for common failure modes, postmortem expectations, on-call rotation rules, game day plans, and status / customer communications templates. It is intended for SREs, service owners, product engineers, and support staff who participate in incident handling and customer communications.

Key principles
- Safety first: protect customer data and production stability.
- Triage quickly: restore a safe state before making changes.
- Clear ownership: every active incident has a named incident commander (IC).
- Communicate frequently: internal and external stakeholders should be updated on a predictable cadence.
- Learn & improve: every Sev 1/Sev 2 incident must produce a blameless postmortem with corrective action items.

Severity definitions and SLO tie-ins
- Sev 0 / P0 (Critical): Production outage impacting all customers or causing data loss; targeted RTO: 30 minutes.
- Sev 1 / P1 (High): Large degradation for many customers; RTO: 2 hours.
- Sev 2 / P2 (Medium): Degraded functionality for subset of customers or non-critical performance regressions; RTO: 24 hours.
- Sev 3 / P3 (Low): Minor issues, cosmetic bugs, or documentation gaps; handled in normal triage.

Note: SLOs and error budgets are maintained in eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets. Incidents that risk SLO burn must be escalated to the Reliability Lead.

On-call roles and responsibilities
- Primary Oncall (Pager): First responder; acknowledges alerts within 10 minutes and performs initial triage.
- Secondary Oncall (Escalation): Engages if Primary cannot resolve within escalation windows (30 minutes for P0, 90 minutes for P1).
- Incident Commander (IC): Coordinates the incident response, owns communication cadence, assigns runbook tasks. IC is elected by the first responder when incident is classified as P1/P0.
- Subject Matter Experts (SMEs): Owners for specific services (e.g., serving-runtime, routing, KV-cache) who execute deep-fix tasks.
- Communications Lead: Prepares external updates (status page, customer emails) and coordinates with Legal/PR for sensitive incidents.
- Postmortem Author: Typically the IC or a delegated engineer; produces the final report within 7 business days for P0/P1.

Alerting and acknowledgement flow
1. Alert triggers (PagerDuty / Alertmanager / Cloudwatch) -> Primary oncall is paged.
2. Primary acknowledges within 10 minutes. If no ack, PD escalates to Secondary after 10 minutes.
3. Primary performs triage: identify affected services, scope, potential rollback/fallback.
4. If incident meets P1/P0 criteria, IC role is assigned and an incident channel is created (#inc-<service>-<YYYYMMDD>-<id>).
5. IC runs runbook (see below) and maintains internal updates every 15 minutes for P0, 30 minutes for P1.

Triage checklist (first 15 minutes)
- Confirm severity and impact: number of customers, percentage of traffic, data integrity risk.
- Identify scope: regions, models, deployments, API routes.
- Check for recent deploys, config changes, infra maintenance windows.
- Obtain logs/traces: request IDs, span IDs, and recent errors from ops-dashboards.
- If possible, apply mitigation (traffic routing, circuit-breakers, disable feature) to reduce customer impact.

Runbooks (selected canonical examples)
1) API 500s (generation service)
- Symptoms: elevated 5xx rate on /v1/generate and increased latency > 4x baseline.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Confirm metric windows (5m, 1h) and correlate with deploys.
  2. Check autoscaler for oom/scale-flapping (GPU OOM).
  3. If model workers are OOM: reduce batch size globally via feature-flag -> rollback recent model or quantization change.
  4. Route traffic to a stable model variant (fallback model) using smart routing policy.
  5. Open a dedicated log query to collect sample request IDs and errors.
- Escalation: page runtime owners (eng-serving-runtime) and infra (eng-infra/gpu-fleet).
- Post-incident remediation: collect heap dumps, kernel logs, update quantization profile if needed.

2) KV-cache mismatch / stale responses
- Symptoms: clients receive stale completions or stateful sessions returning old tokens.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Identify affected deployment and cache shard.
  2. Evict suspect keys from KV-store (admin console command) and enable read-through bypass.
  3. If cache corruption suspected, failover to primary DB and switch read path.
  4. Disable aggressive prefix-caching until investigation completes.
- Escalation: page cache owner and DB on-call.

3) Provisioning/Capacity shortage (Dedicated/GPU provisioning)
- Symptoms: queuing, long wait times, or capacity exceeded errors for Dedicated customers.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Check capacity dashboards and autoscaler logs.
  2. Activate reserved burst capacity policy for affected customer(s).
  3. Turn on temporary rate-limiting for non-critical routes.
  4. Notify Sales/Customer Success for impacted customers and follow customer comms template.
- Escalation: capacity-planning and infra leads.

Runbook conventions
- Every runbook has: symptoms, immediate mitigations (first 30-60 minutes), escalation path, owner list, and post-incident checks.
- Keep runbooks idempotent and include CLI/console commands, sample queries, and rollback steps.
- If a runbook requires >1 hour of manual intervention, produce a play-by-play log into the incident channel.

Escalation timing summary
- P0: Primary 10m ack -> escalate to Secondary 10m -> IC assigned within 20m.
- P1: Primary ack 10m -> Secondary as needed at 30-60m -> IC often assigned within 60m.
- If any data-loss suspicion -> immediate org-wide paging and Legal/Privacy notified.

Communication cadence
- Internal: P0 every 15 minutes; P1 every 30 minutes; include impact, mitigations, next steps, owner.
- External (status page): Initial notice within 30 minutes for P0/P1; updates aligned with internal cadence or minimum every 60 minutes until resolved.
- Customer comms: Use templated messages (see templates section). Personalized outreach for affected enterprise customers via Customer Success within first 2 hours.

Status page & customer comms templates
- Status page entries must be concise and factual. Avoid speculation. Use the following structure:
  - Title: [Service] - Degraded/Outage
  - Impact: Short sentence of what’s affected (who/how many).
  - Status: Identified / Investigating / Mitigating / Resolved
  - Started: ISO timestamp
  - Next update: in XX minutes
  - What we are doing: short bullets of mitigation steps
  - Contact: support@redwood.ai or Customer Success rep for enterprise customers

Sample initial status page message:
  Title: Hosted API - Partial Outage
  Impact: Some customers are receiving 500 errors for text generation endpoints.
  Status: Investigating
  Started: 2026-03-01T11:12:00Z
  Next update: in 30 minutes
  What we are doing: Rolling back a recent model deployment to restore stable workers; routing traffic to fallback pool.

Customer email template (initial):
  Subject: Redwood Inference — Incident affecting hosted API (started 2026-03-01T11:12Z)
  Body: Hello <CustomerName>,

  We are investigating an incident affecting the Hosted API generation endpoints that may cause elevated errors or latency. Our engineers have identified the likely cause and are taking steps to mitigate impact. We will provide updates via our status page: https://status.redwood.ai and directly in this thread. For urgent support, reply to this email or contact your Customer Success rep.

  Sincerely,
  Redwood Support Team

Postmortem policy and template
- Policy: All Sev 0/1 incidents require a blameless postmortem within 7 business days and a public summary (internal) within 48 hours. Actions must be tracked in the company tracker and assigned an owner and target completion date.
- Postmortem sections (flat list):
  1. Title and incident ID
  2. Summary (one-paragraph)
  3. Severity, start/stop timestamps, duration
  4. Impact (customers affected, SLO impact)
  5. Root cause analysis (timeline + cause chain)
  6. Mitigations and immediate fixes taken
  7. Long-term remediation plan (owner + due date per action)
  8. Follow-ups and monitoring changes
  9. Lessons learned

Example postmortem bullet excerpt:
  - Root cause: A quantized-kernel regression introduced in model-compiler v2.1.4 caused OOMs during certain sequence-length distributions.
  - Immediate mitigation: Rollback to v2.1.2 and route traffic to fallback model pool.
  - Corrective actions: Add canary perf test for quantized kernels (owner: Maya T., due 2026-03-15), add GPU memory metrics to alerts (owner: Diego A., due 2026-03-10).

On-call rotations and scheduling rules
- Rotation length: 1 week for Primary oncall; 2 week shadow/secondary rotations are optional for large teams.
- Shift handoff: Each oncall must publish a handoff note to #oncall-handoffs channel with current incidents, outstanding follow-ups, and expected maintenance windows.
- Time off and swap policy: Use the oncall-swap form in the HR portal; swaps must be posted 24 hours in advance unless emergency.
- Backup coverage: For holidays or extended PTO, ensure a secondary cover is assigned at least 72 hours prior.

Game days (exercise & readiness)
- Objective: Validate runbooks, alerting fidelity, and communication processes; surface unclear ownership and tooling gaps.
- Frequency: Quarterly per major service (serving-runtime, routing, infra).
- Roles: Game Day Lead, IC, Oncall participants, SMEs, Observability engineer, Communications observer.
- Typical scenario: Introduce a simulated model crash and capacity loss; exercise: triage, route to fallback, issue customer communications, run post-run retro.
- Deliverables: Game day report with findings, runbook updates, and action items (tracked as tickets).

Incident tooling and dashboards (references)
- PagerDuty: primary incident paging and oncall schedules.
- Ops Dashboards: Grafana service-specific dashboards (latency, error rates, GPU memory, queue depth).
- Tracing: Jaeger for request flows and span IDs.
- Logs: Centralized log queries in Kibana/Elasticsearch.
- Incident tracker: Jira project RED-INC for formal incident postmortems and action items.

Metrics & alert thresholds (examples)
- API 5xx rate > 1% sustained over 5 minutes -> P1 alert.
- API latency: p95 > 3x baseline for 5 minutes -> P1.
- Model worker OOM -> P0 if rate > 10% of workers.
- Queue depth > 1000 pending requests for 10 minutes -> P1.

Post-incident reviews and continuous improvement
- Weekly incident review meeting: Review last 7 days of incidents, track recurring themes.
- Reliability initiatives: Higher-severity incidents generate cross-team projects prioritized in eng-roadmap.
- Documentation ownership: Service owners must verify runbooks quarterly and after any major change.

Appendices
A. Quick pager commands (CLI)
- PD acknowledge: pd ack <incident-id>
- Evict cache: admin-cache evict --service <svc> --key <key-pattern>
- Route to fallback: routerctl promote --pool fallback --service <svc>

- Serving runtime owner: Priya Nair (priya@redwood.ai)
- GPU fleet lead: Diego Alvarez (diego@redwood.ai)

C. Templates & links
- Status page editor: https://status.redwood.ai/admin
- Incident Jira template: RED-INC-Template
- Oncall swap form: https://hr.redwood.ai/oncall-swap

If you are responding to an active incident and need help: page eng-sre@pagerduty and start an incident channel with a short summary.

Document maintenance
- Owner: engineering (oncall program).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any Sev 1/Sev 0 incident.
- To propose edits: open a PR against this page and add reviewers from the reviewers list.

End of playbook.
